questions.q: List four specific physical details of the Pearson living-room mentioned in the opening stage directions that establish the play's setting.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Small suburban semi-detached villa, (2) Two doors — one leading to front door/stairs, one to kitchen/back door, (3) Muslin-covered window(s) in left/right walls, (4) Fireplace in fourth wall, (5) Settee up right, armchairs down left and down right, (6) Small table with two chairs on either side at centre. A wrong answer reveals the student skims stage directions instead of treating them as textual evidence; they may confuse the setting with a generic "living room" without noting the specific spatial arrangement that enables entrances/exits crucial to the plot.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the "early autumn afternoon" timing contributes to the play's atmosphere before any dialogue begins.
questions.a: Correct answer: Early autumn suggests transition and change — summer's ease ending, winter's hardness approaching — mirroring Mrs. Pearson's impending transformation. Afternoon light ("well lit") creates visibility for the audience but also a domestic, routine feel that makes the supernatural personality swap more jarring. A wrong answer treats time as mere backdrop ("it's just when it happens") missing how Priestley uses seasonal symbolism to foreshadow thematic change; students often overlook that "afternoon" implies the family will return soon, creating dramatic tension.

questions.q: The stage direction states: "It is very important that these two should have sharply contrasting voices." Apply this to the setting-atmosphere relationship: how does the physical intimacy of the small table setting amplify the atmospheric tension of the fortune-telling scene?
questions.a: Correct answer: The small table forces Mrs. Pearson and Mrs. Fitzgerald into close physical proximity — knees nearly touching, hands able to reach across — which intensifies the atmospheric intimacy and power imbalance. The confined space traps Mrs. Pearson, making Mrs. Fitzgerald's dominance ("pulls her down," "Gimme your hands") feel physically coercive, not just verbal. The contrast in voices (light/flurried vs. deep/sinister) reverberates in this small room, creating auditory atmosphere that mirrors the psychological pressure. A wrong answer describes the table as just "where they sit" missing how spatial constraints generate atmospheric claustrophobia essential to the scene's power dynamic.

questions.q: Analyze how the atmosphere shifts in the living-room from the moment Doris enters (p.18) to Cyril's exit to the kitchen (p.22). Identify three specific textual markers of this shift.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Doris's "astounded" reaction to smoking/playing cards — visual/auditory disruption of expected domestic atmosphere; (2) Mrs. Pearson's "cool and incisive" manner replacing "fluttering and apologetic" — tonal shift from submissive to authoritative; (3) Cyril and Doris's "huddle... rapidly whispering" then "guffawing and giggling" — shift from tension to nervous mockery, revealing their misreading of the new atmosphere. A wrong answer lists plot points ("Doris asks for tea, Cyril asks for things") without analyzing how each interaction alters the room's emotional climate; students often confuse character actions with atmospheric effect.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the single setting (unity of place) strengthens or weakens the play's social critique. Justify with two pieces of evidence from the text.
questions.a: Correct answer: Strengthens. Evidence 1: The living-room as "much lived-in" by the mother but "enjoyed" by the family becomes a microcosm of gendered domestic labor — the same space where she works invisibly becomes the stage for her rebellion. Evidence 2: All confrontations occur in this one room, forcing George, Doris, and Cyril to face Mrs. Pearson (and each other) without escape — the confined space amplifies the accountability the play demands. A wrong answer claims unity of place limits the play ("we don't see the club, the workplace") missing Priestley's deliberate theatrical choice: the home IS the battlefield, and keeping us there forces focus on domestic power dynamics.

questions.q: Create a new stage direction for the final scene (after Mrs. Fitzgerald leaves) that uses setting details to visually reinforce the restored harmony. Include at least two specific props or spatial arrangements.
questions.a: Strong answer example: "The living-room is warmly lit. The tea things are cleared; the card table is folded away. The settee cushions are straightened. A rummy box sits open on the centre table, cards being dealt. Two armchairs face each other comfortably — no longer opposing sides. The kitchen door stands open, sounds of clinking plates and laughter drifting in. The fireplace burns steadily." A poor answer writes a plot summary ("they play rummy and are happy") without using stage-direction conventions (present tense, visual/spatial focus, prop placement) or connecting props to thematic resolution (cards = family game, open kitchen door = shared labor).
